lesson.title: To Pool or Not to Pool: Handling Unequal Variances
lesson.summary: Two-sample t-procedures come in a pooled version, which assumes the two populations share a common variance, and an unpooled (Welch) version, which does not; modern practice defaults to unpooled even when the sample variances look similar.
lesson.body:
The two-sample t-test in the previous section used what is called the unpooled, or Welch, approach: it estimates the standard error using s1 squared over n1 and s2 squared over n2 separately, without ever assuming the two population variances are equal. There is an older alternative, the pooled t-procedure, which does assume the two populations share one common variance and combines both samples' information into a single pooled estimate. The pooled variance is sp squared equals ((n1 minus 1) times s1 squared plus (n2 minus 1) times s2 squared) divided by (n1 plus n2 minus 2). The standard error becomes sp times the square root of (1 over n1 plus 1 over n2), and because pooling uses one combined variance estimate rather than two conservative pieces, the degrees of freedom is exact: n1 plus n2 minus 2, no approximation needed.

Why does AP Statistics, and most modern statistical practice, default to the unpooled version even when sample standard deviations look close? Because equal population variance is a strong claim that is rarely something you actually know to be true ahead of time. If the assumption happens to be right, the unpooled method is only slightly less efficient than pooling, a small, safe cost. If the assumption is wrong, the pooled method can give a misleading standard error and an unreliable p-value. Statistical software defaults to unpooled for exactly this reason, and that is the procedure to reach for by default unless a problem explicitly tells you the population variances are equal.

It helps to see both methods run on the same numbers. Reusing the caffeine example: n1 equals n2 equals 10, s1 equals 20, s2 equals 25. Pooled variance is ((9)(400) plus (9)(625)) divided by 18, which is (3600 plus 5625) divided by 18, or 9225 divided by 18, equal to 512.5. The pooled standard error is the square root of 512.5 times (1 over 10 plus 1 over 10), which is the square root of 512.5 times 0.2, or the square root of 102.5, about 10.124. That is exactly the same value the unpooled formula gave. This is not a coincidence: whenever the two sample sizes are equal, the pooled and unpooled standard errors are algebraically identical, since averaging the two variances (what pooling does when n1 equals n2) and adding them separately (what the unpooled formula does) land on the same number. The two methods only start to disagree on the standard error itself when the sample sizes are unequal.

Where the two methods do differ here is degrees of freedom, and that changes the critical value and p-value even though the test statistic is identical. Pooled df is 10 plus 10 minus 2 equals 18, versus the unpooled conservative df of 9 used earlier. The one-tailed critical value at alpha equals 0.05 with df equals 18 is 1.734, smaller than the df equals 9 value of 1.833. Working out the p-value at df equals 18 for our test statistic of about negative 1.98: the table gives 1.734 for a tail area of 0.05 and 2.101 for 0.025, and our statistic falls between them, giving a p-value of roughly 0.03. Both approaches reject H0 at alpha equals 0.05 in this case, but the pooled version reports a smaller, more optimistic p-value because it spent extra degrees of freedom on an assumption, equal population variances, that was never verified.

The practical rule: use the unpooled, Welch-style procedure as your default two-sample t-test and t-interval. Recognize the pooled procedure when you see it in software output or older textbooks, and know why its extra precision comes at the cost of a riskier assumption.
